deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is Gauss's working sheet for the definitive Pallas orbit from the six oppositions of 1803, 1804, 1805, 1807, 1808 and 1809. Those are exactly the oppositions treated in his 'Disquisitio de elementis ellipticis Palladis' (Comm. Gott. 1810/11), so the sheet probably dates from about 1810, despite the bundle name 1805.

Header. The 'Normalelemente' for epoch 1803.156 are:
- inclination i = 34°37'47"
- node Ω = 172°28'32"
- eccentricity angle φ = 14°12'51" (e = sin φ)
- perihelion longitude π = 121°7'54"

The working is laid out in six columns, one per opposition. The per-opposition values of Ω, i, π and φ differ slowly from column to column. They are the normal elements with the (Jupiter) perturbations or secular changes applied for each date.

Block A: from heliocentric longitude to true anomaly.
- Row 1 is the observed heliocentric ecliptic longitude λ at opposition (e.g. 277°38'59.17").
- Row 2 is Ω(t).
- Row 3 is λ−Ω. Check: 277°38'59.17" − 172°28'32.43" = 105°10'26.74".
- Row 4 is i(t).
- Then the log-table rows: log tan(λ−Ω) (n = negative), log cos i, log sin(λ−Ω), log tan i.
- Heliocentric latitude: tan β = tan i · sin(λ−Ω). Column 1: 9.9845881 + 9.8392388 = 9.8238269, giving β = +33°41'6.30". These β are compared with the values on the previous page.
- Argument of latitude: tan u = tan(λ−Ω)/cos i. Column 1: u = 102°34'48.33".
- Orbital longitude l = u + Ω = 275°3'20.76".
- Then π(t) = 121°7'53.99".
- True anomaly v = l − π = 153°55'26.77".
- Then φ(t) = 14°12'47.43".

Block B: from true anomaly to mean longitude.
- Row '135020' is −log cos φ in units of the 7th decimal (log cos 14°12'47" = −0.0135020).
- Next rows:
  - log e = log sin φ (9.3901051);
  - log cos v;
  - e cos v (column 1: 1 − 0.22054…; columns 3 and 6: 0.15366926 and 1 − 0.12003);
  - log(1 + e cos v), i.e. log(p/r);
  - log sin v;
  - ½ log(1 + e cos v);
  - log sin v − ½ log(1 + e cos v);
  - log sin(φ/2) (9.0924244).
- These implement the Theoria Motus formula sin ½(v−E) = sin(φ/2) · sin v · √(r/p), giving v − E. Column 1: 7°3'45.91".
- Hence the eccentric anomaly E = v − (v−E) = 146°51'40.86".
- Check on E: log sin v − log(1 + e cos v) = 9.7512247. Subtracting 135020 gives log sin E = 9.7377229, i.e. sin E = cos φ sin v/(1 + e cos v).
- log(e in arcseconds) = log sin φ + log 206264.8 = 4.7045301.
- So e sin E = 27685.54" = 7°41'25.54".
- Mean anomaly M = E − e sin E = 139°10'15.32" (Kepler's equation).
- Mean longitude L = M + π = 260°18'9.31".
- A perturbation term is applied with the sign convention 'subtract the tabulated value'. Column 1: 260°18'9.31" − 4.73" = 260°18'4.58". Column 2: +31.97". Column 3: +5'5.57". Column 4: +8'58.70". Column 5: +8'31.62". Column 6: +20'55.90".

Block C: epoch mean longitude and residuals.
- Subtract the mean motion times the elapsed time, n·Δt. The tabulated values are 5°21'23.07", 96°48'51.21", 194°29'47.18", 306°4'7.10", 402°15'9.09" and 492°46'16.75", with Δt ranging from about 25 to about 2302 days.
- This gives the epoch mean longitude from each opposition: 254°56'41.51", 38.10", 47.58", 42.41", 50.65", 47.64".
- A second row (41.41, 36.35, 44.07, 36.88, 43.38, 38.74) differs from the first by −0.0039"·Δt(days). This is recomputation with the corrected mean motion n = 770.7372"/day (bottom of page), about 0.004"/day larger than the value used first (about 770.733"/day; inferred by me).
- Their mean is L0 = 254°56'40.14".
- Residuals: +1.27, −3.79, +3.93, −3.26, +3.24, −1.40. Their sum is −0.01, consistent with the least-squares condition for the epoch.
- The notes δi = −1" and δΩ = −2.5" record small corrections to inclination and node from the latitude comparison on the preceding page.

The whole page is the reduction of six oppositions to residuals in mean longitude (and latitude), as input to the correction of the Pallas elements.
errors: Column 1: log sin v − ½log(1+e cos v) computed from the page's own numbers is 9.6430194 − 9.9458973½ = 9.6971220½, whereas 9.6971229½ is written (overwritten digits). The effect on v−E is at most about 0.05", so it is immaterial, and it may be a reading issue.
No other arithmetic slips were found in the checked chains (λ−Ω, u+Ω, l−π, v−(v−E), M, M+π, perturbation application, epoch subtraction, residuals).

results.what: Heliocentric latitude and argument of latitude from heliocentric longitude via tan β = tan i sin(λ−Ω) and tan u = tan(λ−Ω)/cos i
sin ½(v−E) = sin(φ/2) sin v √(r/p); sin E = cos φ sin v/(1+e cos v); M = E − e sin E
results.modern_name: true → eccentric → mean anomaly conversion (Kepler's equation)
results.usually_credited_to: Kepler; the half-angle form is in Gauss, Theoria Motus (1809)

results.what: Reduction of six Pallas oppositions (1803–1809) with perturbed elements to an epoch mean longitude, mean motion 770.7372"/day and residuals summing to zero
results.modern_name: orbit determination/differential correction by least squares
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Disquisitio de elementis ellipticis Palladis (1810)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a numerical working sheet for Gauss's well-known Pallas orbit from six oppositions (published 1810, the source of his least-squares elimination). The method and context are well documented as his; only the specific intermediate numbers are unpublished detail.

checkable.asserts: tan β = tan i sin(λ−Ω), column 1 (≈0)
v−E from sin ½(v−E) formula, column 1 (≈0)
e sin E in arcseconds, column 1 (≈0)
residuals sum to ~0 (epoch L0 is their mean)
